rate.gpu.ultra: A current GPU encoder: fast, high-quality 10-bit HEVC. It can work through roughly 15 films a day.
rate.gpu.high: A good GPU encoder: 10-bit HEVC with B-frames. Around 8 films a day.
rate.gpu.medium: An older GPU encoder: it works, but needs more bits for the same quality and is slower.
rate.gpu.low: No GPU encoder found: everything runs on the CPU, which is much slower.
rate.cpu.ultra: Plenty of cores: a 2-hour 1080p film in about an hour on the Medium preset.
rate.cpu.high: 16 or more threads: a 2-hour 1080p film in about 2 hours on Medium. Fine for the occasional grainy film.
rate.cpu.medium: 8 to 15 threads: a 2-hour film takes 3 to 5 hours. Use it for a few films, not for the whole library.
rate.cpu.low: Fewer than 8 threads: a CPU encode takes most of a day. Better leave the CPU fallback off.
rate.subs.ultra: 12 GB of VRAM or more: Whisper's best model (large-v3) runs at full speed, a film in a few minutes.
rate.subs.high: 8 to 12 GB of VRAM: large-v3 runs well; a film takes a few minutes.
rate.subs.medium: 6 to 8 GB of VRAM: it works, but a smaller Whisper model (medium) is faster.
rate.subs.low: Whisper is not installed on this worker, or there is too little VRAM: subtitles only come from OpenSubtitles.
rate.llm.ultra: 24 GB of VRAM or more: room for a 27B translation model next to Whisper, the best quality.
rate.llm.high: The chosen model fits in VRAM next to Whisper. Good translations at a good speed.
rate.llm.medium: The model fits, but only just: Whisper and the translator take turns, so subtitles take longer.
rate.llm.low: The model does not fit in VRAM: Ollama runs it on the CPU, which is very slow. Pick a smaller model.
rate.llm.none: No translation model set in worker.ini: missing subtitles are only searched, not made.
rate.srv.high: The server only scans, checks and swaps files: one core and 1 GB of memory are enough.
rate.srv.disk: Free space on the media share is below your safety brake: encoding is paused until there is room.
rate.cpu.unknown: This worker has not reported its hardware yet; the verdict follows after its next update.
rate.subs.unknown: Whisper is installed, but the worker could not read the amount of VRAM (no NVIDIA tool found), so speed is unknown.
rate.llm.unknown: The worker could not read the amount of VRAM, so whether the model fits is unknown.
rate.cpu.off: CPU encoding is switched off for this worker. Switch it on on the Workers page to use it for grainy films.
rate.subs.off: Subtitles are switched off for this worker, or Whisper is not installed. Switch it on on the Workers page.

tools.ffmpeg: reads, encodes and writes the video files
tools.libvmaf: Netflix's quality score: checks every new file against the original
tools.nvenc: the encoder on an NVIDIA GPU (HEVC 10-bit)
tools.qsv: the encoder on an Intel GPU (HEVC 10-bit)
tools.amf: the encoder on an AMD GPU (HEVC 10-bit)
tools.x265: the CPU encoder, used for grainy films
tools.whisper: turns speech into text, on your own machine
tools.ollama: translates subtitles with a local language model
tools.opensubtitles: existing subtitles, matched on the file's fingerprint
tools.ffsubsync: checks and fixes the timing of found subtitles
tools.mkvtoolnix: turns DVD and Blu-ray folders into one .mkv
tools.dovi_tool: converts Dolby Vision profile 7 to 8.1, so Plex and TVs can play it
tools.vaapi: the encoder on an Intel or AMD GPU under Linux (HEVC 10-bit)

q.q: What is VMAF, and what does 96.5 / 93 mean?
q.a: VMAF is a score from 0 to 100 for how much a new file looks like the original. Netflix made it, and it predicts what real people see. **96.5** is the average over the whole film. **93** is the lowest score the weakest 5% of frames may get, so one dark or fast scene cannot slip through. Above 96 almost nobody sees a difference on a TV. 95 is still very good. 97.5 is for people who sit close to a big screen.

q.q: Why is there a minimum bitrate if the quality score is already fine?
q.a: The score is a little too kind to film grain and to flat, dark scenes. An encoder can smooth the grain away and still get a good score, but on a big TV you would notice. The minimum bitrate (5 Mbps for 1080p, more for 4K, less for SD and animation) keeps enough bits for grain and shadows. It is never higher than 90% of what the original uses.

q.q: How does MediaScan find the right setting for a film?
q.a: It cuts 8 short pieces out of the film and encodes them at a few quality settings, measuring the score each time, until it finds the smallest file that still meets your target. Then it encodes the whole film with that setting and measures it again. Only when that passes, and the file is at least 10% smaller, the original is replaced.

The film was tested, but could not be made smaller while keeping the quality. Often it is already efficient (HEVC at a low bitrate), or it is so grainy that keeping the grain costs more bits than the original has. The original stays as it is. For grainy films the CPU fallback can help.
If a new file would only be a few percent smaller, swapping it is not worth the risk or the time. Below this percentage (10% by default) the original is kept.

q.q: GPU or CPU: what is the difference?
q.a: The GPU has a special chip for video encoding. It is 10 to 20 times faster than the CPU and leaves the rest of the machine free, so it does the bulk of the library. The CPU encoder (x265) is slow, but much better at keeping **film grain**: it can keep the grain at a far lower bitrate. MediaScan only uses the CPU for films the GPU cannot shrink without losing quality.

q.q: What do the CPU presets Medium and Slow do?
q.a: The preset is how hard the encoder searches for savings. **Medium**: about 2 hours for a 2-hour 1080p film on 8 cores. **Slow**: 2 to 3 times longer, for files that are roughly 5 to 10% smaller. The quality target is the same for both; only the time changes.

q.q: Does a CPU encode slow down everything else?
q.a: No. The CPU encoder gets all cores but two, and runs at a lower priority: the GPU work, the dashboard and the rest of the computer keep their room. While a CPU encode runs, the GPU job's quality measurement uses fewer threads, so the two never fight over the same cores.

q.q: Which graphics card do I need?
q.a: A GTX 1660 Super or RTX 2060 is the minimum. Older GTX 10 cards can encode HEVC too, but slower and with worse quality per bit. RTX 20 and 30 cards do it well; RTX 40 and 50 cards are the fastest and give the best quality per bit. Intel Arc and recent AMD cards work too, and so do Apple M-series chips. For subtitles, the amount of VRAM matters: 8 GB is comfortable, 12 GB or more is ideal.

groups.t: Subtitles and the local language model

q.a: First MediaScan asks OpenSubtitles for subtitles that match your exact file. Found ones are checked against the audio and shifted if the timing is off. If nothing fits, Whisper listens to the audio on your own machine and writes down what is said, and Ollama translates that into your languages. Nothing leaves your network except the OpenSubtitles search.

q.q: Which Ollama model should I use?
q.a: The default **gemma4:12b** needs about 9 GB of VRAM and translates well in all 38 languages. With 24 GB of VRAM you can use a 27B model for slightly more natural sentences. With 8 GB, pick a model of 7 to 9B. A model that does not fit in VRAM runs on the CPU and becomes painfully slow.

q.q: Which Whisper model should I use?
q.a: **large-v3** is the most accurate and needs about 5 GB of VRAM. With less VRAM, 'medium' is a good second choice. Whisper also tells which language is spoken, so it works for films in any language.
Next to the film, as a separate file: 'Film.en.srt', 'Film.nl.srt' and so on. Plex and every player pick those up automatically. The film file itself is not touched for subtitles.

No. The new file is written next to the original, checked again on the NAS (length, number of tracks), and only then swapped in. The original goes to quarantine for 7 days (or until the quarantine is full), and can be restored with one click. Audio, subtitles, chapters and HDR information are copied exactly.
When the free space on your media share drops below this amount, encoding pauses by itself, so a full disk can never break anything. It starts again when there is room.

q.q: What happens when a worker goes offline?
q.a: A job that was running goes back into the queue after 10 minutes and another worker (or the same one, later) picks it up. Nothing is replaced until a new file has been checked in full.

errors.staging: The new version was no longer on the NAS when it was time to swap it in (the staging folder was emptied, or the share dropped). **Retry** encodes it again.
errors.mux: One of the tracks in this file cannot go into an .mkv as it is (an unusual subtitle or audio format). The file stays as it is; remux it with another tool first if you want it encoded.
errors.space: The worker's PC has too little free space for this film: it needs about twice the file size plus 20 GB. Free up space and **Retry**.
errors.share: The worker lost its connection to the media share while working. Check the share and **Retry**.
errors.ollama: Ollama (the translation model) did not answer. Is Ollama running on the worker and is the model downloaded? Then **Retry**.
errors.translation: The translation model kept giving unusable answers for a few lines. Usually a one-off: **Retry**.
errors.opensubtitles: OpenSubtitles could not be reached or the daily limit was hit. The job is retried later by itself.
errors.whisper: Speech recognition could not run: no audio track, or Whisper is not installed on the worker (see the Info page).
errors.dv: Dolby Vision films are not re-encoded: the DV layer would be lost. The file stays as it is.
errors.vmaf: The quality measurement of the whole film did not add up (often a file with a variable frame rate). **Retry** measures it again; if it keeps failing the original is kept.
errors.probe: The file could not be read: it may be corrupt or not a video. Check it on the NAS.
errors.original: The original changed or disappeared while the new version was being made, so it was not replaced. **Retry** when the file is stable again.
errors.check: The final check on the NAS found a different duration or track count than expected, so the original was kept. **Retry** encodes it again.
errors.worker: The worker went offline or restarted during this job. It is back in the queue automatically.
errors.ffmpeg: ffmpeg stopped with an error (the text below). Often a damaged source file; **Retry** once, otherwise check the file.
